newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cities report continued fiscal improvement.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cities report continued fiscal improvement.

text.p: For the fifth consecutive year, a growing percentage of U.S. cities say they can better meet their financial needs than a year ago, and most cities also are more optimistic about the future, a new study released Monday found.

Fifty-six percent of the cities who responded to the annual survey by the National League of Cities said they were increasing capital expenditures and 55 percent said they were increasing the growth rate of their operating budgets.
Sixty-eight percent said they were better able to meet their financial needs than one year ago, up sharply from about 35 percent just four years ago.
More than one third, or 36 percent, said they were planning to increase their municipal workforce, while 29 percent reported increased service levels, and 24 percent reported growth in productivity.
While favorable conditions and careful budgeting allowed 14 percent of cities to reduce property tax rates, 32 percent reported higher fees or taxes in order to keep their budgets in balance.

The proportion of hard-pressed cities continued to decline, but one third of the cities described their fiscal conditions as worse than a year ago, and nearly one third reported that general fund expenditures exceeded revenues.
"Most of our cities and towns have a lot of reasons to celebrate," said NLC President Mark Schwartz, a councilmember in Oklahoma City.

"Their finances are stronger, they are providing services more efficiently, and they are taking steps to make the repairs, improvements and new investments needed to be attractive, safe and productive places for people to pursue the American dream," he said.
Infrastructure needs and efforts to enhance public safety topped the list of pressure points on municipal budgets for all cities, regardless of size, according to the survey.

Federal environmental mandates and the effects of state restrictions on local government finances, the overall impacts of prices and cost-of-living, along with the growing cost of employee health benefits were also cited as pressure points.

The 228 cities in the NLC survey included 30 of the 51 largest U.S. cities, 51 percent ofthe cities with populations above 100,000, and 34 percent of cities with populations between 50,000 and 100,000.
